Note::split¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signatures¶

TokenBatch Note::split(std::string_view delim) const
TokenBatch Note::split(std::string_view delim, std::int64_t limit) const

Split Each Cell On A Literal Delimiter¶

split(delim) cuts each text cell at every occurrence of the literal string delim and returns the pieces as a TokenBatch. It is the delimiter-exact structural splitter — the right tool for CSV-ish fields, key:value pairs, a -> b arrows, and other formats with a known separator. When the boundary is “any run of whitespace,” use split_whitespace; when it is a line break, use split_lines; when it is a pattern, use regex().split().

delim is matched literally (no regex) and must be non-empty — an empty delimiter throws pluss::Error. It may be more than one character (" -> " is a single four-byte delimiter).

Empty fields are kept¶

split is a field splitter, not a token filter. Consecutive delimiters, a leading delimiter, and a trailing delimiter each produce an empty piece: "a,,b" splits into "a", "", "b", and ",lead" splits into "", "lead". A cell that does not contain delim yields one piece: the whole cell. (Use split_whitespace, which collapses runs, when empty fields are noise.)

limit¶

limit caps the number of splits, not the number of pieces. After limit splits the rest of the cell is emitted as one final piece: split(",", 2) on "a,b,c,d" gives "a", "b", "c,d" (2 splits, 3 pieces). limit = 0 emits the whole cell unsplit; a negative limit (the default) means unlimited.

The TokenBatch result¶

All pieces from all cells are concatenated into the rank-1 Note batch.tokens(). The rank-1 Int64 Note batch.offsets() has length numel + 1 and marks each cell’s run: cell r owns tokens.at(k) for k in [offsets[r], offsets[r + 1]). Every cell contributes at least one piece, so no offset range is empty.

Example 1: Comma-Separated Fields¶

const auto batch = pluss::make_note({"a,b,c", "x,y", "solo"}).split(",");

std::cout << pluss::note::print(batch.tokens()) << "\n";
std::cout << "offsets: [";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < batch.offsets().integers().size(); ++i)
  std::cout << (i ? ", " : "") << batch.offsets().integers()[i];
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[6], dim=1, numel=6, encoding=utf8)
["a", "b", "c", "x", "y", "solo"]
offsets: [0, 3, 5, 6]

Cell 0 → [0, 3), cell 1 → [3, 5), cell 2 (no comma) → [5, 6), one piece.

Example 2: Empty Fields Are Preserved¶

const auto batch =
    pluss::make_note({"a,,b", ",lead", "trail,"}).split(",");

std::cout << pluss::note::print(batch.tokens()) << "\n";
std::cout << "offsets: [";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < batch.offsets().integers().size(); ++i)
  std::cout << (i ? ", " : "") << batch.offsets().integers()[i];
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[7], dim=1, numel=7, encoding=utf8)
["a", "", "b", "", "lead", "trail", ""]
offsets: [0, 3, 5, 7]

The doubled comma, the leading comma, and the trailing comma each yield an empty piece.

Example 3: A Multi-Character Delimiter¶

const auto batch =
    pluss::make_note({"left -> right -> end"}).split(" -> ");
std::cout << pluss::note::print(batch.tokens()) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["left", "right", "end"]

Example 4: Delimiter Absent¶

const auto batch = pluss::make_note({"no delimiter here"}).split(";");
std::cout << pluss::note::print(batch.tokens()) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["no delimiter here"]

Example 5: Capping The Number Of Splits¶

const auto batch = pluss::make_note({"a,b,c,d,e"}).split(",", 2);
std::cout << pluss::note::print(batch.tokens()) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["a", "b", "c,d,e"]

Two splits, so three pieces; everything after the second comma stays in the last piece.

Example 6: An Empty Delimiter Is Rejected¶

try {
  pluss::make_note({"x"}).split("");
} catch (const pluss::Error& e) {
  const std::string msg(e.what());
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

split: delimiter must be non-empty
